awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Universal models of self-organized criticality
awd_abstract_narration:
Fractals and power-law tails are ubiquitous in nature and are also the hallmarks of statistical physics systems at criticality. Theoretical physicists in the late 1980s proposed that this could be explained by natural systems spontaneously converging to critical states. This theory of self-organized criticality is widely accepted by physicists based on their simulations of simple mathematical sandpile models, which appear to self-organize. But these models are poorly understood mathematically and in some cases have been proven to behave contrary to physicists' expectations. This project aims to establish that activated random walk serves as a suitable mathematical model for self-organized criticality with the universality expected by physicists, and to investigate its behavior. The results of this project will be important not just to mathematicians but to physicists as well. This project involves graduate and undergraduate students.

Activated random walk and the stochastic sandpile model are two of the mathematical models thought to exhibit self-organized criticality. One concrete goal of the project is to prove the density conjecture for activated random walk in dimensions two and higher.  We will do this by establishing that the driven-dissipative version of activated random walk converges to the critical density of the fixed-energy version. We will also study the mixing time of the driven-dissipative activated random walk in all dimensions and determine critical exponents of activated random walk. Finally we will establish similar results for the stochastic sandpile model.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Over its one-year span, this project has advanced our understanding of self-organized criticality through its analysis of activated random walk, which is the best and most universal model for self-organized criticality.

We have completed and published our proof of Rolla's conjecture in dimension 1 that activated random walk is explosive, i.e., that a single active particle has nonzero probability of initiating an infinite cascade of activity in a supercritical, ergodic environment, demonstrating the robustness of the supercritical environment and further establishing the model's suitability. We proved that in a subcritical 1-d environment, the amount of activity at each site has a stretched exponential tail, making for an interesting comparison of the model with other models of self-organized criticality. We proved that on a finite graph, the model rerandomizes and remixes as particles are added to it much more quickly starting from an already mixed state than it does starting from an empty configuration. We led a team of undergraduate researchers at the NYC Discrete Math REU in a very successful project determining how the density of the model on a finite interval evolves in time when particles are added at a location other than the center (to be submitted for publication shortly). In joint work with an undergraduate student, we provided a new proof using more modern theory of a theorem of Rolla's providing a lower bound on the critical density of activated random walk in dimension one for small sleep rates (to be submitted for publication shortly). In addition to these results, we have made progress toward many larger conjectures. Beyond the intellectual merit of these results, our work has had broader impact in its training of graduate and undergraduate students. The PI had a graduate student complete his dissertation on activated random walk and begin a tenure-track job. One undergraduate from the College of Staten Island (CUNY) contributed to this research, as did two undergraduates (from the University of Virginia and the University of Chicago) participating in the NYC Discrete Math REU.
